  4. If you downloaded the ZIP from the Talkwyn download page, click Upload Plugin instead, choose the file, and activate it.

2. Scan your site

  1. Open Talkwyn in the dashboard menu.
  2. Click Scan my site.
  3. Wait for the scan to finish. Larger sites take a little longer.

Talkwyn reads your published pages, posts, menus, custom fields, Elementor content, and WooCommerce products (price, stock status, and attributes). It never reads drafts, users, or passwords. After the first scan, it keeps the index up to date when you edit content.

3. Connect an AI key

  1. Create a key with Groq, Google Gemini, OpenRouter, or Cloudflare Workers AI.
  2. In Talkwyn's AI provider settings, add the provider and paste the key.
  3. Add a second provider if you can, and put your favorite first.
  4. Save.

Several providers offer free tiers. Their limits are set by each provider and change over time. With two providers, Talkwyn switches automatically when one hits its limit. See choosing an AI provider for where to get each key.

Tip: paste keys only into Talkwyn's settings. Never put a key in a page, a post, or a public file.

4. Customize the chat window

  1. Pick a color that matches your site.
  2. Choose an avatar.
  3. Write a welcome message that says what visitors can ask, for example "Ask me about prices, opening hours, or delivery."
  4. Choose where the chatbot appears. Hide it on checkout, thank-you, or any page where it would distract.

5. Go live and test

  1. Turn the chatbot on and save.
  2. Open your site in a private browser window.
  3. Ask a question you know the answer to, like your opening hours.
  4. Check that the answer is right and that a source link appears under it.
  5. Ask a follow-up, like "and how much is that?"
  6. Ask something your site does not cover. Talkwyn should say it does not know and offer to connect the visitor with your team.
  7. Ask a question in another language your customers use.

If an answer is wrong or missing, update the page that should answer it. Talkwyn picks up the change.

6. Check lead capture

When a visitor shows buying intent, such as "can I book?" or "call me", Talkwyn asks if they want a follow-up, then shows a short form inside the chat. Leads are saved in WordPress and emailed to you instantly.

  1. Make sure lead capture is on in Talkwyn's settings.
  2. Check the email address where leads are sent.
  3. Send a test lead from your site and confirm the email arrives.
  4. Export leads as CSV any time from the Talkwyn leads screen.

7. Start a Pro trial (optional)

The free plan is free forever. To try paid AI models, advanced search, analytics, and the inbox, start a free Pro trial. You get every Pro feature for [tw_value key="trial_days"] days on one site. [tw_value key="trial_card_policy"] When it ends, upgrade with the same key or keep the free plan.

8. Activate a license key

  1. Copy your license key from your account's licenses page.
  2. In WordPress, go to Talkwyn, then Settings, then License.
  3. Paste the key and click Activate.
Staging and local sites do not count toward your site limit, so you can test changes safely.

Troubleshooting

The chatbot does not answer

  • Check that the chatbot is turned on and not hidden on the page you are testing.
  • Check that at least one AI provider has a saved key. Create a new key if you are not sure it is valid.
  • Add a second provider in case the first has reached its free limit.

An answer is wrong or out of date

  • Find the page that should hold the answer and make sure it is published, not a draft.
  • Update the text on that page. Talkwyn refreshes its index when you edit.
  • Remove old or conflicting copies of the same information from other pages.

Lead emails are not arriving

  • Check the lead email address in Talkwyn's settings.
  • Look in your spam folder, and mark the message as safe.
  • Leads are also saved in WordPress, so nothing is lost while you fix email delivery.

For more on the plugin itself, see the WordPress chatbot plugin page. Stuck on a step? Contact the Talkwyn team and tell us which step did not work.

title: Choosing an AI provider and getting a free AI API key
excerpt: Where to get a free AI API key, how to add two for automatic fallback, and which paid models Talkwyn Pro adds.
content:
Talkwyn does not charge per conversation. It sends each question to an AI provider you choose, and several providers give you a free AI API key with a free tier. This page shows where to get each key, how to add two for automatic fallback, and what Pro adds.

Which free AI API key should you pick?

All four free options work well for a small business chatbot. The best setup is two of them from different companies, so one can cover for the other.

  • Groq: a simple first choice, known for fast replies.
  • Google Gemini: a good second provider, from a different company.
  • OpenRouter: one key for models from many companies, some marked as free.
  • Cloudflare Workers AI: handy if you already use Cloudflare. Needs an Account ID and a token.
Free limits are set by each provider and change over time. We do not list them here. Check each provider's own limits page for the model you plan to use.

Is a free AI API key enough? For many small business sites, yes, for everyday questions. A sale, a busy season, or a burst of traffic can push a single free tier over its limit, which is why we recommend two providers from the start. If you outgrow free tiers, you can add a paid key from the same provider, or move to one of the paid models in Pro. Nothing else in your setup has to change: your content, chats, and leads stay where they are.

Groq

  1. Go to console.groq.com/keys and sign in.
  2. Create a new API key and name it, for example "My website chatbot".
  3. Copy the key. It is shown only once.
  4. In Talkwyn's AI provider settings, add Groq and paste the key.

Google Gemini

  1. Go to aistudio.google.com/app/apikey and sign in with a Google account.
  2. Create an API key.
  3. Copy the key.
  4. In Talkwyn, add Gemini and paste the key.

OpenRouter

  1. Go to openrouter.ai/settings/keys and sign in.
  2. Create a new key and copy it.
  3. In Talkwyn, add OpenRouter and paste the key.
  4. Choose a model. Check on OpenRouter which models are free today.

Cloudflare Workers AI

  1. Sign in to the Cloudflare dashboard.
  2. Copy your Account ID.
  3. Create an API token with permission to use Workers AI, and copy it.
  4. In Talkwyn, add Cloudflare and paste both the Account ID and the token.

Add two providers for automatic fallback

  1. Add your first provider and paste its key.
  2. Add a second provider from a different company and paste its key.
  3. Put your favorite provider at the top of the list.
  4. Save, then ask your chatbot a question to confirm it answers.

The order Talkwyn tries providers

  1. Greetings and small talk are handled without calling any AI, so they do not use your quota.
  2. For other questions, Talkwyn tries the provider at the top of your list.
  3. If that provider hits its limit or is busy, Talkwyn moves to the next one and remembers which one is working.
  4. If every provider is busy, Talkwyn still replies with the most relevant information it found on your site.

Change or remove a provider

  1. Open Talkwyn's AI provider settings.
  2. To replace a key, paste the new key over the old one and save.
  3. To change the order, move the provider you want first to the top of the list.
  4. To remove a provider, delete it from the list and save. Then delete the key on the provider's own site too.

Troubleshooting

  • The key is rejected. Copy it again with no spaces before or after. If it still fails, create a new key on the provider's site.
  • Cloudflare does not connect. Check that you pasted both the Account ID and the token, and that the token is allowed to use Workers AI.
  • Answers stop at busy times. Your free tier may have hit its limit. Add a second provider from a different company.
  • Replies in one language are weak. Language quality depends on the model. Try another provider or model and test again.
  • An OpenRouter model stopped working. The list of free models changes. Pick another model marked as free, or a paid one.

Paid models with Pro

Talkwyn Pro adds OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, Mistral, and DeepSeek. Paid models are a good choice for busy sites, for steady capacity in peak seasons, or for the best quality in a less common language. Language quality depends on the model you choose, so test your main languages. See Talkwyn pricing, or try Pro free for [tw_value key="trial_days"] days.

Privacy

Messages go only to the AI provider you picked. Talkwyn does not send them anywhere else. Your indexed content, chats, and leads stay in your own WordPress database. Only public, published content is indexed, and you can turn logs off or delete them automatically after a set number of days. Each provider has its own privacy terms, so read them before you choose.

Keep your keys private. Paste them only into Talkwyn's settings. If a key leaks, delete it on the provider's site and create a new one.

Hotels and travel

A hotel chatbot that answers guests before they book

Talkwyn is a hotel chatbot for hotels, guesthouses and travel businesses. It reads your room, rate, policy and local guide pages, then answers guests in their own language at any hour. When a guest wants to book or has a special request, it takes their details and emails your front desk.

[tw_icon name="check" size="14"] New lead saved

Guests plan trips at night, from other time zones

A traveler is comparing three hotels at 2 am their time. They want to know if breakfast is included, whether pets are allowed, and how far you are from the station. The answers are on your site, spread across the rooms page, the policies page and the location page. If nobody answers, they book the hotel that made it easy.

Your front desk hears the same questions every day: check in times, parking, airport transfers, cancellation rules, late check out. Each one is quick, but together they pull staff away from the guests standing in the lobby.

And your guests come from everywhere. Some write in German, French, Spanish or Arabic, and they are more likely to book when they get an answer in their own language.

One scan, and your rooms, policies and local tips become answers.

[tw_icon name="eye-off"]

Stays off your booking pages

Hide the chatbot on booking, payment or thank-you pages, so nothing distracts a guest at the last step.

A hotel chatbot example in German

A guest writes in German. Talkwyn answers in German from the hotel's English pages, keeps prices exactly as listed, and hands the availability question to the front desk.

English translation

  1. Hello, is there a transfer from the airport?
  2. Yes. According to our getting here page, the hotel offers an airport shuttle for 25 € per trip. Please book it 24 hours in advance.
  3. And can I bring my dog?
  4. Yes, small dogs are allowed in selected rooms. The fee is 20 € per night.
  5. Do you have a double room free from May 12 to 15?
  6. Unfortunately I can't check availability. Leave your name and email address, and the front desk will get back to you.

This is an example conversation with a made-up hotel. Answers come from that hotel's own pages. See the German chatbot for websites page for more on German replies.

Die Verfügbarkeit kann ich leider nicht prüfen. Hinterlassen Sie Ihren Namen und Ihre E-Mail-Adresse, dann meldet sich die Rezeption bei Ihnen.

Set up your hotel chatbot the right way

A chatbot is only as good as the pages it reads. A few choices before you go live make the difference between a helpful assistant and a confusing one.

  • Publish what guests ask. Check in and check out times, parking, breakfast, pets, airport transfers and the cancellation policy. Talkwyn can only answer what your pages say.
  • Keep rates and offers current. If a page still shows last season's prices, the chatbot will quote them. Edit the page and the index updates.
  • Do not expect it to confirm availability or take payments. It answers questions and collects booking requests. Your team or your booking system handles the rest.
  • Hide it on booking and payment pages with the hide-on-page setting.
  • Ask guests not to share card numbers or passport details in the chat. A request only needs a name and a way to reach them.
  • Test it in the languages your guests use before you turn it on for everyone.

Chats and leads stay in your own database. You can turn logs off, or have them deleted after a number of days you choose.

No. Talkwyn answers from your published pages and does not see your booking calendar. When a guest asks about dates, it collects a booking request and emails it to your team.

No. It handles the routine questions your pages already answer, and hands interested visitors to your team.

Talkwyn is a restaurant chatbot for restaurants, cafes and bakeries. It reads your menu, opening hours, location and events pages, then answers guests in their own language, day and night. When someone wants a table for a group or a private event, it takes their details and emails you.

It is 7:30 on a Friday. The kitchen is full, every table is taken, and the phone keeps ringing. Are you open on Sunday? Do you have vegan options? Is there parking? Can you seat twelve people next week? Every call pulls someone away from a guest who is already there.

Most of those questions are answered on your website. Your menu, your hours and your directions are already published. People just do not read them on a small screen while they decide where to eat.

Visitors and tourists add another layer. They may write in French, Spanish, Italian or Arabic, and a quick answer in their own language is often what tips the choice your way.

A restaurant chatbot example in French

A visitor writes in French. Talkwyn answers from the restaurant's English menu and allergen page, and sends the allergy question back to the team.

English translation

  1. Hello, do you have vegetarian dishes?
  2. Yes. The menu has four vegetarian dishes, including the mushroom risotto at $18.
  3. Does the risotto contain nuts?
  4. According to the allergen page, the risotto contains no nuts, but it is prepared in a kitchen that uses nuts. If you have an allergy, please tell the team.
  5. I would like to book for 6 people on Saturday evening.
  6. With pleasure. Leave your name and number, and the restaurant will call you back to confirm the table.

What to set up, and what to avoid

Restaurants change fast: menus, specials, holiday hours. These steps keep your chatbot accurate.

A chatbot for law firms that handles the practical questions

Most calls to a law office are not legal questions

Do you handle immigration cases? How much is a first consultation? Is there parking near the office? Does anyone speak Spanish? These are the questions that fill a receptionist's day. They are practical, and the answers are usually already on your website.

People looking for a lawyer are often stressed and in a hurry. Many search in the evening, after work, and contact the first firm that answers. A form that promises a reply in two business days can lose them.

A chatbot for law firms can answer those practical questions at any hour, point people to the right practice area, and pass serious enquiries to your team, without ever acting like a lawyer.

  5. Are there lawyers who speak Spanish?
  6. Yes, the team page says two lawyers work in Spanish. If you like, leave your name and phone number and the office will call you to book the consultation.

What a chatbot for a law firm should and should not do

Talkwyn is not a legal tool and must not be used to give legal advice, assess a case, or predict an outcome. It answers practical questions from your own published content: practice areas, hours, location, fees you publish and how to book a consultation.

Set it up with care:

  • Publish a clear page explaining that chat messages are not legal advice and do not create a lawyer and client relationship. Talkwyn can then point visitors to it.

  • Test it before going live. Ask questions about a specific case and check that the replies send people to a consultation.
  • Turn chat logs off, or set them to delete automatically after a number of days you choose.
  • Check your bar's or regulator's rules on advertising and client communication with your own advisor.

Talkwyn does not claim any legal industry certification. Chats and leads stay in your own database, and messages go only to the AI provider you pick.

title: Multilingual Website Chatbot Guide: Serve Every Visitor Without Translating Your Whole Site
excerpt: How a multilingual website chatbot answers visitors in their own language from content you wrote once, and how to prepare your site for it.
content:
A multilingual website chatbot lets you help visitors in their own language even if your site is written in only one. You write your pages once, and the chatbot reads them and answers each question in the language the visitor used. This guide explains how that works, what to prepare, and where a full translation still makes sense.

On this page

  1. The problem with translating every page
  2. How a multilingual website chatbot works
  3. What to prepare on your site first
  4. Which languages to focus on
  5. When you still need translated pages
  6. Set it up on WordPress

The problem with translating every page

Translating a whole website is a big job. Every service page, product description, policy, and blog post needs a version in each language. Then every change you make later needs to be made again in every version. For a small team, that often means the translated pages fall behind, and visitors end up reading old prices or old policies.

Many visitors do not need a full translated site anyway. They need one or two answers: Do you ship to my country? How much is this? Are you open on Saturday? If they can ask in their own language and get a clear reply, they can keep going.

That is the gap a multilingual chatbot fills. It does not replace good translation for your most important pages. It covers the long tail of questions in languages you could never afford to translate for.

How a multilingual website chatbot works

Here is what happens when a visitor writes to a multilingual website chatbot like Talkwyn:

  1. The visitor types a question in their own language.
  2. The chatbot detects the language of that message.
  3. It searches your published content for the answer, even though your pages are in a different language.
  4. It writes the reply in the same language the visitor used, with links to the pages it used as sources.
  5. If the visitor switches language halfway through the chat, the chatbot switches with them.

Some details stay exactly as they are. Names, prices, email addresses, and product names are not translated, so a visitor sees the same product name they will see on the checkout page. Messages that mix two languages in one sentence are handled too, which is common for people who speak more than one language at home.

Talkwyn focuses on 12 popular languages: English, Spanish, French, German, Portuguese, Italian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and Turkish. More languages work too, depending on the AI model you choose. You can see how it handles each one on the multilingual chatbot page.

What to prepare on your site first

The chatbot can only answer from what you published. Good source pages matter more than the number of languages. Before you turn it on, check these:

  • Shipping and service areas. Visitors from other countries ask about delivery first. Say clearly where you ship or serve, and where you do not.
  • Prices and currencies. State which currency your prices are in. The chatbot keeps prices as written, so make sure they are correct and current.
  • Contact options. List your email, phone, and hours, including your time zone.
  • Policies in plain sentences. Returns, refunds, cancellations, and booking rules are easier to answer when they are written as short, clear sentences.
  • One answer per question. If two pages disagree, fix that first. A chatbot that finds two answers cannot know which one is right.

Our guide on how to write pages your chatbot can answer goes deeper into page structure. The same advice helps in every language.

Which languages to focus on

You do not need to pick languages in advance. The chatbot replies in whatever language a visitor writes in. Still, it helps to know which languages your visitors use so you can test those first.

  • Check your analytics for visitor countries and browser languages.
  • Look at the emails and messages you already get. Which languages show up?
  • Ask your team which languages customers use on the phone or in the shop.
  • Think about where you want to grow, not only where you are today.

Then test each of those languages yourself, or ask a native speaker you trust to try it. Each language has its own page with examples, for instance the Spanish chatbot, French chatbot, and Arabic chatbot pages.

Language quality depends on the AI model you pick. If a language matters a lot to your business, test it with real questions on your own site before you rely on it.

How to test a language you do not speak

You can still check the basics without being fluent. Write your test questions in English first, then ask a native speaker, a customer you know well, or a staff member to type them in their language the way they would naturally say them. Ask them three things about each reply: Does it sound natural? Is the answer the same as on your page? Are names and prices unchanged? Keep notes, fix any page that caused a weak answer, and test again.

When you still need translated pages

A chatbot is not a full replacement for translation. There are cases where translated pages are still the right call:

  • Search visibility. If you want to rank in search for queries in another language, you need real pages in that language.
  • Legal and checkout text. Terms, contracts, and payment steps are often better as carefully translated pages, reviewed by a person.
  • Your main market. If most of your customers speak a second language, give them a full experience in it.

There is also a middle path. Some sites translate only the homepage and the contact page, so visitors from other countries feel welcome right away, and then rely on the chatbot for detailed questions. That keeps the translation work small while still giving people a clear first impression in their language.

A practical approach for many small businesses: translate the few pages that matter most, and let the chatbot cover everything else. If you do run a translated site with WPML or Polylang, Talkwyn's interface text, such as the welcome message and button labels, can be translated with those plugins too.

Set it up on WordPress

Talkwyn is live today as a WordPress chatbot plugin. Setup takes about five minutes:

  1. Install Talkwyn from your dashboard: Plugins, Add New, search "Talkwyn".
  2. Click "Scan my site" so it reads your published pages, posts, and products.
  3. Paste a free AI key from a provider like Groq or Google Gemini.
  4. Pick your color, avatar, and welcome message.
  5. Turn it on, then ask it a question in each language you care about.

The getting started guide covers each step with screenshots. Multilingual answers are part of the free plan, so you can try it without paying anything. Plans are listed on the pricing page if you later want paid AI models or analytics.

Multilingual website chatbot FAQ

Do I need to translate my website for a multilingual chatbot?

No. The chatbot reads your pages in the language you wrote them in and replies in the visitor's language. You may still want translated pages for search or legal text.

Which languages does Talkwyn support?

Talkwyn focuses on 12 popular languages, including Spanish, French, German, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, and Japanese. More languages work too, depending on the AI model you choose.

What if a visitor switches language during the chat?

The chatbot detects the language of each message and switches with the visitor. Mixed messages that change language mid-sentence are handled as well.

Will it translate my prices and product names?

No. Names, prices, emails, and product names stay exactly as written on your site, so visitors see the same details at checkout.

How good are the answers in less common languages?

That depends on the AI model you choose. Test your key languages with real questions before launch, and consider a paid model if quality matters a lot.

How long does setup take?

About five minutes. Install Talkwyn, click Scan my site, paste an AI key, pick your color, avatar and welcome message, and turn it on. The setup guide walks through each step.

How does the free trial work?

You get every Pro feature for [tw_value key="trial_days"] days on one site. [tw_value key="trial_card_policy"] When the trial ends, upgrade with the same key or keep the free plan. Start the trial.

What happens when the answer is not on my site?

Talkwyn says it could not find that and offers to connect the visitor with your team. It answers business questions only from your own content, so it never invents a price or a policy.

Where are chats and leads stored?

In your own website database. Messages go only to the AI provider you picked, and you can turn chat logs off or have them deleted after a number of days you choose. Read our privacy approach.

Do I need to pay for AI?

Not to get started. Groq, Google Gemini, OpenRouter and Cloudflare Workers AI offer free tiers. Add more than one and Talkwyn switches automatically when one hits its limit. Pro adds OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, Mistral and DeepSeek. Choose an AI provider.

title: Chatbot vs Contact Form: When Each One Works Best on Your Website
excerpt: An honest look at when a website chatbot beats a contact form, when it does not, and how the two can work side by side.
content:
The chatbot vs contact form question comes up for almost every small business site. Both let visitors reach you, but they solve different problems. A form collects a message for later. A chatbot answers questions right now. This guide helps you decide which one your site needs, and when the honest answer is both.

On this page

  1. What each tool is really for
  2. When a chatbot beats a contact form
  3. When a contact form is the better choice
  4. Chatbot vs contact form side by side
  5. How to use both together
  6. Questions to ask before you decide
  7. Try a chatbot without removing your form

What each tool is really for

A contact form is a mailbox. The visitor writes a message, clicks send, and waits for a reply. It works well when the visitor already knows what they want to say and is happy to wait.

A website chatbot is closer to a helpful person at the front desk. The visitor asks a question and gets an answer in seconds, drawn from your own pages. If the question needs a human, the chatbot can collect their details and pass them on.

So the real question is not which one is better. It is what your visitors need at the moment they reach out.

Think about the last twenty messages that came through your form. How many asked something your website already explains? How many needed a real conversation with someone on your team? That split is a good first clue for the chatbot vs contact form decision on your own site.

When a chatbot beats a contact form

A chatbot tends to help more in these situations:

  • The question already has an answer on your site. Opening hours, prices, delivery areas, and return rules are faster to answer than to email about. The visitor gets the answer, and your inbox stays quiet.
  • The visitor is deciding right now. Someone comparing you with another business may not wait a day for a reply. A quick answer can keep them on your page.
  • Visitors write in different languages. A multilingual chatbot replies in the visitor's own language. A form gives you a message you may need to translate before you can reply.
  • Questions come in outside office hours. A chatbot answers at night and on weekends from your published content.
  • The visitor is not sure what to ask. A chat lets people ask follow-up questions, like "and how much is that?", until they find what they need.

When a contact form is the better choice

A chatbot is not the right tool for everything. A plain form often works better when:

  • You need structured details. Quote requests with measurements, file uploads, or many required fields are easier in a well designed form.
  • The request is long or personal. Job applications, complaints, and detailed project briefs suit a form where the visitor can take their time.
  • Your site has very little content. A chatbot answers from your pages. If those pages are thin, a form plus a fast human reply may serve visitors better until you add more content.
  • Every question needs a person. If nothing can be answered without looking at a specific account or case, a chatbot adds a step instead of removing one.
Rule of thumb: if most messages in your inbox could be answered by a page you already have, a chatbot will help. If most need a human decision, keep the form front and center.

Structured fields and uploadsShort lead form onlyYes, as many as you need
Setup effortInstall, scan your site, add an AI keyBuild and style the form

Neither column is always better. The right mix depends on what your visitors ask and how your team works.

What about response time on your side?

A form only works as well as your follow-up. If messages sit in an inbox for days, visitors notice. A chatbot does not fix slow follow-up on leads, but it does remove the wait for simple questions, which leaves your team more time for the requests that need them. Whichever you choose, decide who checks new messages and how often.

How to use both together

Most small business sites end up with both, and that is fine. Here is a simple setup that avoids overlap:

  1. Keep your contact page with its form for detailed requests.
  2. Add a chatbot to the rest of your site to answer quick questions from your content.
  3. Let the chatbot offer a short lead form when someone is ready to book, buy, or wants a call back.
  4. Point the chatbot to your contact page for requests that need a long message or files.
  5. Review both inboxes for a few weeks and adjust your pages based on what people ask.

With Talkwyn, the lead form appears inside the chat only after the chatbot asks the visitor if they want to share their details. Leads are saved in WordPress and emailed to you right away, and you can export them as CSV. See the lead generation features for details, and our tips on turning chats into leads without being pushy.

Questions to ask before you decide

  • What are the ten questions we hear most, and are the answers on our site?
  • How long do visitors wait for a reply today?
  • Which languages do our customers use?
  • Do most requests need files, measurements, or account details?
  • Who on the team will follow up on leads, and how fast?
  • Do we have pages for shipping, pricing, and policies, or are those only in our heads?

If the answers point to quick questions, many languages, and slow replies, a chatbot is worth a try. The small business chatbot page shows how this looks for local service businesses.

Try a chatbot without removing your form

You do not have to choose on day one. Install the free WordPress chatbot plugin, keep your contact form where it is, and watch which questions the chatbot handles. Setup takes about five minutes with the getting started guide. If you want analytics and an inbox later, compare plans on the pricing page.

Usually not. Keep the form for detailed requests and add a chatbot for quick questions. Most sites work best with both.

title: How to Write a Chatbot FAQ Page, Pricing and Policy Pages That Answer Well
excerpt: Practical writing tips for FAQ, pricing and policy pages so an AI chatbot can find and quote the right answer.
content:
An AI chatbot is only as good as the pages it reads. A clear chatbot FAQ page, a pricing page with plain numbers, and policies written in short sentences make the difference between a helpful answer and a vague one. This guide shows you how to write those pages so both visitors and your chatbot can find what they need.

On this page

  1. Why your pages decide your answers
  2. How to write a chatbot FAQ page
  3. How to write a pricing page
  4. How to write policy pages
  5. Structure that helps any chatbot
  6. Keep pages current after launch
  7. Test your pages with real questions

Why your pages decide your answers

Talkwyn answers business questions only from your own published content. It does not make up prices or policies. When it cannot find an answer, it says so and offers to connect the visitor with your team.

That is a good thing, but it means gaps in your pages show up as gaps in your chatbot. If your refund rules live only in your head, the chatbot cannot share them. If your prices are inside an image, it may not see them. The fix is not a smarter chatbot. It is clearer pages.

The good news: pages that work for a chatbot also work for people. Short sentences, clear headings, and one answer per question help everyone.

How to write a chatbot FAQ page

A FAQ page is often the fastest way to improve your chatbot. Here is how to build one that works:

  1. Start from real questions. Go through your email, phone notes, and messages. Write down the questions people actually ask, in their words.
  2. Use the question as the heading. "Do you deliver on weekends?" is better than "Delivery". It matches how visitors type.
  3. Answer in the first sentence. Start with yes, no, or the number. Add detail after.
  4. Keep each answer to one topic. If an answer covers delivery and returns, split it into two questions.
  5. Link to the full page. If a longer page covers the topic, link to it. The chatbot shows source links under its answers, so visitors can read more.

An example of a weak and a strong answer

Weak: "We aim to be flexible with our customers and will always try to find a solution that works." This does not answer anything.

Strong: "Yes, you can cancel up to 24 hours before your appointment at no charge. Later cancellations are charged in full." This is an example policy for illustration. Write your own real rules in the same direct style.

How to write a pricing page

Price questions are some of the most common questions a chatbot gets. Make them easy to answer:

  • Write prices as text, not only in images or graphics.
  • Say what is included and what costs extra.
  • Name the currency and whether taxes are included.
  • If prices vary, say what they depend on. "From $80, depending on room size" (an example) is far more useful than "Contact us for a quote".
  • Keep one price in one place. If the same price appears on several pages, make sure they all match after every change.

If you sell with WooCommerce, the scan reads product prices, stock status, and attributes directly, so keep those fields filled in. Our post on questions shoppers ask a WooCommerce chatbot covers store pages in detail.

Talkwyn keeps prices exactly as written on your site, in every language. If a price is wrong on the page, it will be wrong in the chat, so check prices first.

How to write policy pages

Returns, refunds, shipping, cancellations, and booking rules are where vague answers cause the most trouble. Write them like this:

  • Use one page per policy, with a clear title like "Returns and refunds".
  • Put the main rule first: the time limit, the condition, and what the customer gets.
  • List exceptions as bullets so they are easy to spot.
  • Use numbers and dates instead of words like "soon" or "a while".
  • Write how to start the process: who to contact and what to include.

Keep the legal wording if you need it, but add a short plain summary at the top. Visitors and chatbots both read the summary first.

Write the exceptions down

Most policy questions are really about exceptions. "Can I return a sale item?" "Do you refund custom orders?" "What if the parcel arrives damaged?" If your policy page only covers the normal case, the chatbot has nothing to say about the edge cases, and it will tell the visitor it does not know. That is honest, but it sends the question back to your inbox. List the exceptions you handle often, with the rule for each.

Structure that helps any chatbot

  • Use real headings, not bold text styled to look like headings.
  • Keep paragraphs short. Two to four sentences each.
  • Avoid hiding key facts in tabs, sliders, or PDFs when a plain section on the page would do.
  • Publish what you want answered. The scan reads published pages, posts, products, menus, custom fields, and Elementor content. It never reads drafts.
  • Update the page, not the chatbot. When you edit a page, Talkwyn keeps its index up to date.

The knowledge base features page explains what the scan reads and how source links work.

Keep pages current after launch

Pages drift. A price changes, a new service is added, holiday hours come and go. Each of those is a chance for an old answer to stay on your site. A few habits help:

  • When you change a price or policy, search your site for the old value and update every page that mentions it.
  • Add seasonal details, like holiday hours, to a single page and remove them when the season ends.
  • Put a short "last updated" line on policy pages so your team knows when they were last checked.
  • Read the questions visitors ask in chat every few weeks. Repeated questions without a good answer show you which page to write next.

This is the same work you would do for visitors reading your site. The chatbot just makes the gaps easier to see.

Test your pages with real questions

title: WooCommerce Chatbot: The Questions Shoppers Ask Before They Buy
excerpt: The pre-purchase questions shoppers ask and how to prepare your WooCommerce store so a chatbot can answer them well.
content:
A WooCommerce chatbot is only useful if it can answer what shoppers actually ask. Most questions before a purchase fall into a few groups: stock, sizes and options, price, shipping, returns, and payment. This guide covers each group and shows you how to prepare your store so the answers are right.

On this page

  1. Why pre-purchase questions matter
  2. Stock and availability
  3. Sizes, options, and fit
  4. Price, discounts, and payment
  5. Shipping and delivery
  6. Returns, exchanges, and warranty
  7. Questions that should go to a person
  8. Prepare your WooCommerce chatbot in one afternoon

Why pre-purchase questions matter

A shopper with an unanswered question has three choices: search your site, email you and wait, or leave. On a phone, with a cart open, searching and waiting both feel like work. A quick answer keeps the decision moving.

A WooCommerce chatbot answers those questions from your store's own data. Talkwyn reads your WooCommerce products, including price, stock status, and attributes, along with your pages, posts, and menus. It shows source links under each answer, so shoppers can tap through to the product or policy.

The questions below come up in almost every kind of store, from clothing to home goods to digital products. For each group you will find typical questions, what your store needs to have in place, and what the chatbot can and cannot do. Use it as a checklist: if a group has no clear answer anywhere on your site, that is the first page to write, whether you add a chatbot or not.

Stock and availability

Typical questions: "Is this in stock?", "Do you have it in blue?", "When will it be back?"

  • Keep stock status accurate in WooCommerce. The chatbot reads it directly.
  • Set up variations for each size or color so availability is clear per option.
  • If you restock on a schedule, say so on the product page or a FAQ page.
  • If you offer back orders or pre-orders, explain how they work in plain words.

The chatbot will not guess a restock date. If you have not published one, it says it does not know and offers to connect the shopper with your team.

Sizes, options, and fit

Typical questions: "What size should I get?", "Is this true to size?", "What material is it?"

  • Fill in product attributes such as size, material, color, and dimensions.
  • Publish a size guide as a page, with measurements written as text.
  • Add care instructions and materials to product descriptions.
  • If items run small or large, say so in the description.

Price, discounts, and payment

Typical questions: "How much is this with shipping?", "Do you have a discount code?", "Can I pay in installments?"

  • Keep regular and sale prices correct in WooCommerce. The chatbot never invents a price.
  • List accepted payment methods on a page, such as your FAQ or checkout help page.
  • If you run promotions, publish the rules and end date on a page while they are active, then remove or update it.
  • Say whether prices include tax.

Talkwyn understands follow-ups, so a shopper can ask about a product and then type "and how much is that?" without repeating the product name.

Shipping and delivery

Typical questions: "Do you ship to my country?", "How long does delivery take?", "How much is shipping?"

  • Publish a shipping page with zones, costs, and delivery times written as text.
  • Say which countries or regions you do not ship to.
  • Explain free shipping thresholds if you have them.
  • Describe how tracking works and when shoppers get it.

Shipping questions often come from visitors in other countries, writing in their own language. Talkwyn replies in the shopper's language while keeping prices and product names exactly as written. See the multilingual chatbot page for how that works.

Returns, exchanges, and warranty

Typical questions: "Can I return this?", "Who pays for return shipping?", "Is there a warranty?"

  • Write your return window as a number of days.
  • List items that cannot be returned.
  • Say who pays return shipping and how refunds are paid.
  • Describe how to start a return, step by step.
  • If products carry a warranty, state who provides it and how long it lasts.

Clear return rules often matter most to first-time shoppers, who do not know your store yet. A short, confident answer about returns can be the thing that gets them to try you.

Tip: hide the chatbot on checkout and thank-you pages if you want a clean, distraction-free payment step. Talkwyn lets you hide it on any page.

Questions that should go to a person

Some shopper questions should not be answered by a chatbot at all, and that is fine. Plan for them so the hand-off feels natural:

  • Order problems. Late parcels, wrong items, or damaged goods need someone who can look at the order.
  • Custom and bulk orders. Quotes for large quantities or personalized products usually need a conversation.
  • Complaints. An upset customer deserves a human reply.
  • Anything not on your site. If you have not published the answer, the chatbot should not guess, and Talkwyn does not.

For these, Talkwyn says it does not know or that your team can help, and offers to connect the shopper with you. If they agree, it shows a short form inside the chat, saves the lead in WordPress, and emails it to you right away. The lead generation features page explains how intent detection works.

Example conversation

Here is an example of how a pre-purchase chat might go on a sample clothing store. It is an illustration, not a real customer.

  • Shopper: Do you have the linen shirt in medium?
  • Chatbot: Yes, the linen shirt is in stock in medium. You can see all sizes on the product page. (Source: Linen shirt)
  • Shopper: and how much is shipping to Canada?
  • Chatbot: Yes, we ship to Canada. The cost and delivery time for Canada are on our shipping page. (Source: Shipping)
  • Shopper: I need 30 for my team, can I get a deal?
  • Chatbot: Our team handles bulk orders. Would you like to leave your name and email so they can get back to you?

Prepare your WooCommerce chatbot in one afternoon

  1. List the questions you get most by email, chat, and phone.
  2. Check that each one has a clear answer on a published page or product.
  3. Fill in missing product attributes and fix stock status.
  4. Write or update your shipping, returns, and payment pages. Our guide on writing pages your chatbot can answer helps here.
  5. Install Talkwyn from Plugins, Add New, click "Scan my site", and add a free AI key.
  6. Ask your list of questions and fix any page that gives a weak answer.

When a shopper is ready to buy in bulk, wants a call, or asks about a custom order, Talkwyn can ask whether they want to share their details and save them as a lead. More on that on the ecommerce chatbot page and the WooCommerce integration page. Plans and Pro features are on the pricing page.

WooCommerce chatbot FAQ

Talkwyn reads published products, including price, stock status, and attributes, plus your pages, posts, menus, custom fields, and Elementor content.

Does it update when I change a product?

Yes. Talkwyn keeps its index up to date when you edit your content.

Can it show order status?

No. Talkwyn answers from public, published content. It does not read customer accounts or orders. Point shoppers to your order tracking page for that.

Will it make up a discount or price?

No. It answers business questions only from your own content and never invents a price or a policy.

Can I hide the chatbot at checkout?

Yes. You can hide it on checkout, thank-you, or any other page.

title: How to Test Your Chatbot Before Launch: A Practical Test Plan
excerpt: A step-by-step test plan to run before you turn on a website chatbot, so the first visitors get good answers.
content:
Before real visitors see it, take an hour to test your chatbot the way a customer would. A short, planned test catches wrong answers, missing pages, and awkward hand-offs while they are still easy to fix. This plan works for any website chatbot, with notes on how each step looks in Talkwyn.

On this page

  1. Why a planned test beats a quick try
  2. Step 1: Build your question list
  3. Step 2: Check answers and sources
  4. Step 3: Test follow-ups and unknown questions
  5. Step 4: Test every language you expect
  6. Step 5: Test lead capture end to end
  7. Step 6: Check design, mobile, and privacy settings
  8. Launch, then keep testing

Why a planned test beats a quick try

Most people test a new chatbot by typing "hi" and one easy question. It answers, and they turn it on. Then the first real visitor asks something slightly different, and the answer is vague or points to the wrong page.

A planned test is different. You decide in advance what to ask, what a good answer looks like, and what you will fix. It takes a little longer, but you launch knowing how the chatbot behaves instead of hoping.

You can run the whole plan before visitors see anything. In Talkwyn, set up your colors, avatar, and welcome message, test, and only then turn it on for everyone.

Step 1: Build your question list

Start with a simple spreadsheet or document with four columns: question, expected answer, source page, and result. Then fill it with questions from:

  • Your email inbox and contact form messages.
  • Phone notes and questions your team hears in person.
  • Your existing FAQ page.
  • Your top pages in analytics: what would someone reading that page want to ask next?

Aim for a mix of easy and hard questions. Include the ones you dread answering, like refunds and complaints. Write some the way customers really type: short, misspelled, without punctuation.

Step 2: Check answers and sources

Ask each question and compare the reply with your expected answer. For every reply, check:

  1. Is it correct? Prices, hours, and policies must match your pages exactly.
  2. Is the source link right? Talkwyn shows source links under each answer. Click them and make sure they lead to the page you expect.
  3. Is it clear? Would a customer understand it without reading the whole page?
  4. Is it complete? Does it answer the question that was asked, not a nearby one?

When an answer is wrong, the fix is almost always on the page, not in the chatbot. Rewrite the page, save it, and ask again. Talkwyn keeps its index up to date when you edit, so changes show up without a new setup. Our guide on writing pages your chatbot can answer has tips for common problems.

Step 3: Test follow-ups and unknown questions

Follow-up questions

Real chats are rarely one question long. Ask about a product or service, then follow up with "and how much is that?" or "do you have it in another size?" A good chatbot understands what "that" refers to. Talkwyn handles follow-ups like these.

Questions your site cannot answer

This is the most important test. Ask things you know are not on your site: a product you do not sell, a service area you do not cover, a discount that does not exist. The chatbot should say it does not know and offer to connect the visitor with your team. It should never invent a price or a policy. Talkwyn is built to do exactly that, but checking it on your own content gives you confidence.

Small talk and off-topic messages

Try "hi", "thanks", and "are you a robot?" Greetings and small talk should get a friendly reply. In Talkwyn they are handled without using your AI quota.

If a test answer surprises you, write down the exact question. The same wording will come up again from real visitors.

Step 4: Test every language you expect

If your visitors write in more than one language, test each one. Ask the same key questions in each language and check that:

  • The reply comes back in the same language as the question.
  • Prices, names, emails, and product names are unchanged.
  • The chatbot switches when you switch language mid-chat.
  • Right to left languages such as Arabic display correctly. See our Arabic chatbot checklist.

Language quality depends on the AI model you choose, so if a language matters a lot, ask a native speaker to review a few answers. The multilingual chatbot page lists the languages Talkwyn focuses on.

Step 5: Test lead capture end to end

Pretend to be a ready customer. Type things like "can I book?", "what's the price?", or "call me". Then check the whole path:

  1. The chatbot asks before showing the lead form.
  2. The form is short and easy to fill in on a phone.
  3. The lead appears in your WordPress dashboard.
  4. The email notification arrives in the right inbox, and not in spam.
  5. Someone on your team knows they are responsible for following up.

Also test the opposite: say no when the chatbot offers the form, and make sure it keeps helping without pushing. Read more on the lead generation features page.

Step 6: Check design, mobile, and privacy settings

  • Mobile. Open your site on a phone. Check that the chat button does not cover important buttons and the chat window is easy to read and close.
  • Where it shows. Decide whether to hide the chatbot on checkout, thank-you, or other pages.
  • Welcome message. Make sure it says what the chatbot can help with, in plain words.
  • Privacy notice and logs. Review the built-in privacy notice, and decide whether to keep chat logs, turn them off, or auto-delete them after a set number of days.
  • AI providers. Add a second provider so Talkwyn can switch automatically if the first one hits its limit.

Our website chatbot privacy checklist covers the privacy side in more detail.

Launch, then keep testing

When your test sheet looks good, turn the chatbot on. For the first few weeks, read new chats regularly. Add any new question to your sheet, fix the page behind any weak answer, and test again. The chatbot gets better because your pages get better.

If you have not installed Talkwyn yet, the getting started guide walks you through setup on the WordPress chatbot plugin. Pro adds analytics and an inbox that make ongoing review easier. Compare plans on the pricing page.

Questions about how to test your chatbot

How long should I test my chatbot before launch?

An hour or two is enough for most small sites. What matters is a planned list of real questions, not the time spent.

How many questions should I test?

Start with the questions you get most, plus a few you know the site cannot answer. Add more as real visitors ask new ones.

What should I do when an answer is wrong?

Fix the page the answer came from, save it, and ask again. Talkwyn updates its index when you edit content.

Should I test in other languages if I only speak English?

Yes, if your visitors use them. Ask a native speaker to type a few questions and review the replies.

Yes. Set it up and test before you turn it on for everyone.

title: Arabic Chatbot Checklist: Right to Left Text, Numbers and Fonts
excerpt: A practical checklist for website owners whose visitors write in Arabic: direction, mixed text, numbers, fonts, and testing.
content:
If some of your visitors write in Arabic, your Arabic chatbot needs more than good translations. Arabic is written right to left, often mixed with English names and numbers, and it needs fonts that stay readable at small sizes. This checklist covers what to look at before launch, whether your site is in Arabic, English, or both.

On this page

  1. Why Arabic needs its own checks
  2. Right to left layout
  3. Mixed Arabic and English text
  4. Numbers, prices, and dates
  5. Fonts and readability
  6. Test with real Arabic questions
  7. Interface text and the rest of your site

Why Arabic needs its own checks

Most chat widgets are designed left to right first. When an Arabic message appears in a left to right layout, punctuation can jump to the wrong end, bubbles can align oddly, and mixed text can become hard to follow. None of this is about the quality of the answer. It is about whether the visitor can read it comfortably.

Arabic speaking visitors also tend to mix scripts naturally: an English brand name inside an Arabic sentence, a phone number, a price with a currency code. A good Arabic chatbot handles all of that without breaking the line.

Talkwyn detects the language of each message, replies in the same language, and displays Arabic right to left with readable fonts. The checks below help you confirm that on your own site, with your own content.

Right to left layout

Open your chat and send a few Arabic messages. Check that:

  • Arabic text starts on the right and reads right to left.
  • Question marks and periods appear at the end of the sentence, on the left side.
  • The chat bubbles line up in a way that feels natural to an Arabic reader.
  • English replies in the same chat still display left to right.
  • Source links under each answer stay readable and clickable.

Mixed Arabic and English text

Mixed text is normal, not an edge case. Test messages like these:

  • An Arabic question that includes an English product or brand name.
  • A message that starts in Arabic and switches to English halfway through.
  • An Arabic question that includes an email address or website.
  • A follow-up in English after an Arabic answer.

Talkwyn keeps names, prices, emails, and product names exactly as written, and it handles messages that switch language mid-sentence. If the visitor switches to English for the next message, the chatbot switches too.

Tip: if your product names have an official Arabic version, publish it on the product page next to the English name. The chatbot can only use names that appear in your content.

Numbers, prices, and dates

Numbers deserve their own test because mistakes here cost money or bookings.

  • Prices. Ask for the price of a few products in Arabic. The amount and currency should match your page exactly.
  • Phone numbers. Check that phone numbers keep their digits in the correct order inside an Arabic sentence.
  • Opening hours and dates. Ask about hours and holiday dates and make sure they read clearly.
  • Digits. Arabic speakers may write with Western digits (1, 2, 3) or Eastern Arabic digits. Try both in your questions to see that the chatbot understands them.

Because prices are kept as written on your site, the most important step is making sure your pages have correct, current prices with a clear currency. Our guide on writing pages your chatbot can answer covers pricing pages in detail.

Fonts and readability

Arabic letters connect and change shape depending on their position in a word. A font that looks fine for English can make Arabic small, thin, or cramped. Check on both a phone and a laptop:

  • Arabic text is large enough to read without zooming.
  • Letters connect properly and do not look broken.
  • Line spacing leaves room for dots and marks above and below letters.
  • Your theme's font choices do not override the chat window in a way that hurts Arabic.

Talkwyn displays Arabic with readable fonts by default. If your theme applies strong custom styles everywhere, take a quick look to make sure the chat still looks right.

Test with real Arabic questions

The best test is a native Arabic speaker using your site the way a customer would. Ask them to:

  1. Ask five to ten common questions about your business, in their own words.
  2. Try at least one question with an English name or a price in it.
  3. Ask something your site does not cover, and check the chatbot admits it does not know.
  4. Try a request like "can I book?" to see the lead form flow in Arabic.
  5. Read each answer and tell you if it sounds natural and matches your pages.

Arabic has many regional dialects, and visitors may write in a dialect rather than formal Arabic. Include a few dialect questions in your test if your customers use them. Language quality depends on the AI model you choose, so if Arabic is important to your business, compare a couple of models. Our full chatbot test plan covers the rest of the launch checks.

Interface text and the rest of your site

The chatbot's replies follow the visitor's language automatically. Interface text, such as the welcome message and button labels, is a separate setting. If you run a translated site with WPML or Polylang, you can translate Talkwyn's interface text with those plugins, so Arabic pages show an Arabic welcome message.

If your site is not translated into Arabic, the chatbot can still answer Arabic questions from your existing pages. See the Arabic chatbot page for example conversations, and the multilingual chatbot overview for the other languages Talkwyn focuses on. title: Website Chatbot Privacy Checklist for Small Businesses
excerpt: A practical website chatbot privacy checklist: what to check before you turn a chatbot on, and what to tell your visitors.
content:
Website chatbot privacy comes down to a few plain questions: what can the bot read, where do the chats go, who can see them, and how long are they kept. This checklist walks through each one so you can set up a chatbot with care, explain it to your visitors, and know what to ask your own advisor.

On this page

  1. 1. Know what the chatbot can read
  2. 2. Keep sensitive content off public pages
  3. 3. Find out where chats and leads are stored
  4. 4. Know which AI provider sees the messages
  5. 5. Set how long logs are kept
  6. 6. Ask for only what you need
  7. 7. Tell visitors what happens
  8. 8. Control where the chatbot appears
  9. A one-page checklist
This is a practical checklist, not legal advice. Privacy rules differ by country and by industry. Check with your own advisor what applies to your business.

1. Know what the chatbot can read

A chatbot that answers from your website has to read your website first. The first privacy question is simple: which content does it read, and which content does it never touch?

  • Does it read only public, published pages, or also drafts and private posts?
  • Can it see user accounts, customer records, or order history?
  • Does it read files you uploaded but never linked, such as PDFs in your media library?
  • Can you exclude a page or a section if you need to?

Talkwyn indexes only public, published content: pages, posts, WooCommerce products, menus, custom fields, and Elementor content. It never reads drafts, users, or passwords. A good rule for any tool: if a page is not something you would show a stranger on your website, it should not be in the chatbot's index. Read more about how Talkwyn answers from your content.

2. Keep sensitive content off public pages

The chatbot only knows what you publish. That is good news, because it gives you a simple control. Before launch, look through your public pages for anything that should not be there:

  • Internal price lists or staff notes left on a forgotten page.
  • Customer names, testimonials with personal details, or case notes.
  • Old pages with outdated policies that you meant to unpublish.

Clinics, law firms, and schools should be extra careful here. Our chatbot for healthcare page has a short list of what a clinic chatbot should and should not do.

3. Find out where chats and leads are stored

Every chat creates data: the questions, the answers, and sometimes a name and phone number. Ask where that data lives.

  • Is it stored on the vendor's servers, or in your own database?
  • Can you export it, for example as CSV?
  • Can you delete a single conversation or lead when someone asks?
  • What happens to the data if you stop using the tool?

With Talkwyn, chats and leads stay in your own WordPress database, and you can export leads as CSV. That keeps the data with the rest of your site data, under the backups and access rules you already use.

4. Know which AI provider sees the messages

An AI chatbot sends each question, along with the relevant parts of your pages, to an AI model to write the answer. That model runs at an AI provider. You should know which one, and read its terms.

  • Which provider receives the messages?
  • Can you choose the provider yourself, or is it fixed?
  • Does the provider's plan you use allow your kind of data?

Talkwyn sends messages only to the AI provider you picked, such as Groq, Google Gemini, OpenRouter, or Cloudflare Workers AI, and on Pro, OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, Mistral, or DeepSeek. Because you choose, you can read that provider's terms and decide. Our guide to choosing an AI provider explains the options.

5. Set how long logs are kept

Chat logs are useful. They show what visitors ask and where your pages fall short. They are also data you have to look after. Decide how long you really need them.

  • Turn logs off completely if you do not need them.
  • Or set them to delete automatically after a number of days you choose.
  • Keep leads separately if your team needs them for follow-up.

Talkwyn supports both: logs can be turned off, or deleted automatically after a set number of days. A shorter period means less data to protect.

6. Ask for only what you need

A lead form inside a chat should be short. Most businesses only need a name and one way to reach the person. Every extra field is more data to store and more reason for a visitor to stop.

  • Ask for a name and a phone number or email, not both unless you need both.
  • Never ask for passwords, card numbers, or ID numbers in a chat.
  • In health, legal, or financial settings, ask visitors not to share details of their case in the chat.

Talkwyn asks before it shows the form, so visitors choose whether to share their details. See how that works on the lead generation chatbot page, and our tips for capturing leads without being pushy.

7. Tell visitors what happens

People are more comfortable when they know what is going on. Be open about it:

  • Show a short privacy notice in the chat window, with a link to your privacy policy.
  • Mention the chatbot, the AI provider, and how long you keep chats in your privacy policy.
  • Make it clear the visitor is talking to an AI assistant, not a person.

Talkwyn includes a built-in privacy notice you can show in the chat. Write the wording with your own advisor so it matches your policy.

8. Control where the chatbot appears

Not every page needs a chatbot. On some pages it can get in the way, or invite people to share things they should not.

  • Hide it on checkout and thank-you pages so it does not distract during payment.
  • Hide it on patient forms, application forms, or pages about sensitive topics.
  • Keep it on pages where questions are practical: services, prices, hours, shipping.

Talkwyn lets you hide the chatbot on checkout, thank-you, or any page you choose. It also has rate limiting built in, which helps stop abuse of the chat.

A one-page checklist

  1. The chatbot reads only public, published content.
  2. No sensitive content sits on public pages.
  3. You know where chats and leads are stored, and you can export and delete them.
  4. You know which AI provider receives messages, and you read its terms.
  5. Logs are off, or set to delete after a period you chose.
  6. The lead form asks only for what you need.
  7. Visitors see a privacy notice and know they are talking to an AI.
  8. The chatbot is hidden on checkout and sensitive pages.

Run through this list before launch, then again whenever you change your site or your provider. Our chatbot test plan covers the rest of the launch checks, and the Talkwyn privacy page explains how we handle data on talkwyn.com.

No. It indexes only public, published content. It never reads drafts, users, or passwords.

In your own WordPress database. Messages go only to the AI provider you picked to write the answer.

title: Lead Capture Chatbot Tips: Turn Chats Into Leads Without Being Pushy
excerpt: How to turn website chats into leads by helping first, asking at the right moment, and following up fast.
content:
A lead capture chatbot works best when it feels like good service, not a toll gate. Visitors come with a question. Answer it well, notice when they are ready to talk to you, and then ask for a name and a number. These tips show how to set that up so more chats turn into real conversations with your team.

On this page

  1. Answer first, ask second
  2. Ask at the moment of intent
  3. Ask before you show the form
  4. Keep the form short
  5. Make sure every lead reaches a person fast
  6. Be honest when the answer is not there
  7. Write a welcome message that invites questions
  8. Measure what matters
  9. Examples by industry

Answer first, ask second

Many chat widgets open with a form: enter your email to continue. A visitor who only wanted your opening hours closes the window. The ones who stay often wait a day for an answer they could have had in seconds.

Turn that around. Let the chatbot answer the question right away, from your own pages. A visitor who got a helpful answer is far more likely to share their details when you ask, because you already showed you are useful.

That only works if the answers are right. Make sure your prices, services, and policies are on your pages in plain words. Our guide on writing pages your chatbot can answer shows how.

Ask at the moment of intent

The best time to ask for contact details is when the visitor shows they want something from you. Phrases like these are clear signals:

  • "Can I book?" or "Do you have time on Saturday?"
  • "What's the price for...?" after a few questions about one service
  • "Can someone call me?" or "I want to talk to someone"
  • Questions about a quote, a viewing, a consultation, or a visit

Talkwyn detects this kind of intent in many languages. When it sees it, it offers a follow-up from your team. It can also offer one after a few helpful replies, so interested visitors who never say "book" still get the option.

Ask before you show the form

Even at the right moment, a form that pops up on its own can feel pushy. Ask a simple question first: "Would you like our team to call you to confirm a time?" If the visitor says yes, then show the form.

This small step keeps the visitor in control. It also gives you better leads, because everyone who fills the form chose to.

Keep the form short

Every extra field costs you leads and gives you more data to look after. For most businesses, two fields are enough:

  • A name, so your team knows who they are calling.
  • One way to reach them: a phone number or an email, whichever you use most.

You do not need to ask what they want. The conversation already says it. A good lead record includes the chat itself, the page the visitor came from, and the question they asked, so your team has context before they reply.

Never ask for passwords, card numbers, or sensitive personal details in a chat. Our website chatbot privacy checklist covers what to keep out.

Make sure every lead reaches a person fast

A lead that sits in a dashboard nobody checks is not a lead. Decide before launch who receives new leads and how quickly they reply.

  • Send leads to an inbox someone reads every day.
  • Agree on a reply time with your team, and stick to it.
  • Call back in the visitor's language when you can. The chat shows which one they used.
  • Export leads as CSV if you work from a spreadsheet or another tool.

Talkwyn saves every lead in your WordPress database and emails it to you instantly. WhatsApp and Slack lead alerts are coming to Pro, along with lead scoring and AI summaries of the conversation.

Be honest when the answer is not there

One of the best moments to capture a lead is when the chatbot does not know. If a visitor asks something your pages do not cover, a guess can lose their trust. An honest "I could not find that, would you like our team to get back to you?" turns a gap into a conversation.

Talkwyn never invents a price or a policy. When the answer is not on your site, it says so and offers to connect the visitor with your team. Then add the missing answer to a page, so the next visitor gets it right away.

Write a welcome message that invites questions

The first line in the chat window sets the tone. A message that asks for an email feels like a form. A message that invites a question feels like help. Try something close to how your best employee would greet a customer at the door.

  • Name the kinds of questions you can answer: prices, opening hours, delivery, bookings.
  • Say that visitors can write in their own language, if your customers speak more than one.
  • Keep it to one or two short sentences, so it does not cover your page on mobile.

Then read your chat logs after the first week. If visitors keep asking the same thing, mention it in the welcome message, and make sure the answer sits clearly on one of your pages. A good welcome message and good pages do more for your lead count than any extra form field. You can change the welcome message, color, and avatar in Talkwyn at any time.

Measure what matters

You do not need complex reporting to improve. Check a few simple things every week:

  1. How many leads came in, and how many your team reached.
  2. Which questions led to a lead, so you know what people really want.
  3. Which questions had no answer, so you can fix those pages.
  4. Which languages visitors used, so you can test those first.

On Pro, chatbot analytics shows which questions had no answer, and the inbox keeps every lead with its conversation. See how the whole flow works on the lead generation chatbot page, and try it on your own site with the WordPress chatbot plugin.

  • Clinics. Answer hours and insurance, then offer an appointment request. See the chatbot for healthcare.
  • Home services. Confirm the service area, then offer a quote visit. See the home services chatbot.
  • Online stores. Answer sizes and shipping, and offer help with larger or custom orders. See the ecommerce chatbot.

When a visitor shows buying intent, such as "can I book?" or "call me", or after a few helpful replies. It asks before it shows the form.

Every lead is saved in your WordPress database and emailed to you instantly. You can export leads as CSV.
